body_markdown:
Leadership in the AI SDLC


Your teams and agents can generate change faster than anyone can steer it.


Linear CEO Karri Saarinen just named a problem most engineering leaders feel but rarely say out loud. Agents and teams can now produce change faster than any leader can understand it, and leadership is quietly losing the ability to steer. Here is what he describes, and what it takes to steer an engineering organization in the AI SDLC.


AC


**Alex Circei** CEO and Co-Founder, Waydev


The problem


## A denial of service, from your own people


In his essay, Saarinen describes how hard it has become to live up to a principle he has written about before: you can outsource work, but not your understanding.


“It feels like our organizations are being DDoSed from the inside.”


Karri Saarinen, CEO of Linear


Nobody is attacking the company. Everyone is doing work they believe is useful. But all of it draws on the same limited capacity to understand, review and decide, and that capacity has not grown at the speed of generation. Saarinen compares it to a car speeding up until it becomes impossible to steer. Leaders never saw every piece of work, but the work can now change the direction of the company faster than leadership can respond.


He is careful to say this is not about people making poor decisions. Linear invests heavily in hiring and in an environment built for good judgment. Even so, he describes unclear or shifting direction and overlapping or conflicting features. Something can go from idea to working implementation before anyone outside the immediate team knows it exists.


The trap


## “It already exists” is not a reason to ship it


When something takes twenty minutes to build, asking to discuss it at tomorrow’s meeting starts to feel unreasonable. Saying “looks good, let’s go” is easier. Saarinen’s answer is the core of the essay: the fact that work exists does not tell you whether it is the right thing to do. We have to stop treating output as proof of value. A working implementation proves something can be built, not that it belongs in the product, and some changes have negative value.


But the opposite extreme fails too. You cannot hold an alignment meeting for every one of the 1,000 pull requests a team might open in a day. Leaders are stuck between rubber-stamping everything and becoming the bottleneck.


**FAILURE MODE 1 · RUBBER STAMP** Approve what already works. Speed stays high, direction drifts, features overlap and conflict.


**FAILURE MODE 2 · BOTTLENECK** Discuss everything before it is built. Direction stays clear, experimentation dies, and you cannot keep up anyway.


**WHAT WORKS · STEERING AT THE SYSTEM LEVEL** Set intent up front, gate what lands in the shared product, and see what all the work adds up to without reviewing each change individually.


What Linear is trying


## Two moves, and one gap


1


**Make intent clear ahead of time** What the company is betting on, what matters now, what is out of scope, written down so people and agents can check their own work against it.


2


**Be deliberate about what lands** Building is cheap; landing in the shared product has consequences. Linear locked down its internal release channel so changes are considered together in one place, while experiments continue behind other flags.


?


**The gap: does it all add up?** Saarinen is candid that the gate helps track what is changing, but does not yet tell him whether all the work adds up to the direction he wants. His closing question: are we moving toward something, or just getting better at reacting?


That gap is the heart of the problem. Intent and gates are inputs. Steering also needs feedback: a continuous, honest picture of where the work is actually going. And it is not just a CEO problem. Saarinen points out that every leader whose judgment you rely on is also trying to keep up with everyone else.


The steering loop


## You cannot steer what you cannot see


Every steering system has the same shape: a direction, an engine, and instruments that show where you are actually heading. Most engineering organizations upgraded the engine with agents and kept the old instruments.


The aggregate view is what turns a pile of individually reasonable changes into something a leader can steer. In practice, it answers questions like these every week, without reading 1,000 pull requests:


1


**Where is the effort actually going?** Work mapped to initiatives and bets, so you can see whether effort matches stated intent, or drifts away from it.


2


**Where are teams and agents overlapping?** Multiple teams or agents changing the same areas of the codebase is the earliest signal of the conflicting features Saarinen describes.


3


**How much is landing, and how much is churn?** Volume of change versus what reaches production and stays there. Output that gets reworked or reverted is the “negative value” made visible.


4


**Is review keeping up?** Review is where the organization’s limited attention gets spent. Track the queue, wait time and depth of[code review](https://waydev.co/?p=8585) before it quietly becomes a rubber stamp.


Trust people, instrument agents


## The answer is not more surveillance of people


Saarinen makes a point worth repeating: he trusts his people, and the problem is not bad decisions. That matters for how leaders respond. The surge of change is driven by agent throughput, not by people suddenly working differently. Watching engineers more closely will not restore steering. Understanding what the agents are producing, where it goes and whether it holds up, will.


That is the direction we have taken at Waydev: measure AI agents, not people. Which agents generate the most change, how much of it lands, how much creates review load or rework, and whether it moves the bets the company actually made. People stay accountable for direction and judgment. The instruments watch the engine.


Agents upgraded the engine of every engineering org. Most leaders are still steering with the old dashboard.


Alex Circei, CEO, Waydev


Intent as context


## Make agents check their work against your intent


Saarinen’s first move, writing intent down so people and agents can check their own work against it, only works if agents can actually read that intent alongside how your organization builds software: ownership, standards, what is in flight, and what broke last time. For most enterprises, that context is too sensitive to send to a public model. So it either never reaches the agents, or it leaks.

## Responsibility does not scale down with speed


Saarinen ends on a point every engineering leader should hold onto: stepping back does not remove responsibility for where it all leads. Each team can make reasonable decisions, and leaders still own what those decisions add up to. In the AI SDLC, the way to keep that responsibility without becoming the bottleneck is not more meetings. It is better instruments, clearer intent, and agents that work inside both.
